blindSummary:
This state/province offers the closest approximation to pockets of refuge in the country: LGBTIQ+ people migrate there to "remake the meaning of home" and find spaces where they feel "valued, accepted and able to be themselves, even if those spaces are hidden and limited." No local enforcement actions, discriminatory bylaws, mass raids, or violence waves have been documented against trans visitors. The unit sits outside the country's set of units with discriminatory local regulations. However, the 2026 national penal code applies equally: a provision criminalises sex outside marriage and cohabitation (up to one year, complaint-based by spouse/parent/child), and broad "indecency" provisions remain; travel guides advise discretion with public displays of affection for all couples. A 2025 ethnographic study of the local third-gender (trans woman) communities explicitly challenges the "romanticised refuge" framing, documenting "resistance and misrecognition" and systemic discrimination even there.

The absence of local enforcement is a practice fact rather than a legal exemption. Compared with larger units elsewhere in the country that saw hotel raids and discriminatory regulations, this unit has a quieter record, but it is not a protected space; the new national penal code and a 2025 government regulation on criminal procedure create fresh exposure that could be activated in any police contact.
